great.name: Melmetal
great.notes: Melmetal has become a unanimous favorite thanks to a major buff to Double Iron Bash. It gives Melmetal a 2 DPE attack at a blazing 4 pace. Dynamic Punch makes for excellent coverage as well. Its stat product is merely average, but its power and pacing more than compensate.

great.name: Altaria
great.notes: Moonblast and Sky Attack are now interchangeable, making Altaria more flexible than ever. Fairy + Fire coverage provides more super effective targets, including the mirror. Against Fire and Water types that resist both, Altaria can usually muscle through those matchups with its superior bulk. Altaria is still vulnerable to Ice, and its pacing a bit on the slower side.

great.name: Shadow Ninetales
great.notes: Kanto Ninetales is a top pick with a Worlds-winning pedigree. Its Energy Ball coverage is so effective that it has warped Water and Ground types around it. The Shadow is almost always preferred. Ninetales struggles against Dragons and rival Fire types, so build your team accordingly.

great.name: Cramorant
great.notes: Cramorant has a similar profile to Pelipper with middle of the road stats and well paced attacks. However, its Fast Attack pressure and special mechanics put it notably ahead of its counterparts. Gulp Missile softens its matchups and even turns some losses into draws. It's become a strong favorite this season despite a steep learning curve. Preference leans toward Dive to get the form change faster, but Surf is also viable.

great.name: Tinkaton
great.notes: Tinkaton is a top meta pick with its immensely powerful signature move, Gigaton Hammer, which even threatens Water types that resist it. The Bulldoze rework gives Tinkaton some closing power, but is also a big pacing nerf. It's likely to remain top meta, although other Fairy or Steel types are vying for its spot.

great.name: Mimikyu
great.notes:
Mimikyu's special ability blocks the first unshielded Charged Attack it receives; its Defense then lowers by 1 stage the rest of the match, even if it swaps out.

This effectively grants Mimikyu a third shield, a massive advantage that far outweighs its drawbacks. It performs best when given shields to delay the debuff.

Mimikyu has seen significant play so far this season without Lickilicky as an omnipresent challenge. Its main drawback is its slow pacing.

great.name: Corviknight
great.notes: Corviknight receives damage buffs to both Air Cutter and Iron Head, improving its neutrals and giving it stronger identity. While its pacing is now slower, it's also less bait and boost dependent. It should be a strong contender going into the season.

great.name: Galarian Corsola
great.notes: Galarian Corsola remains a haunting meta staple, and its prospects improve even more this season with the downfall of Lickilicky. Its bulk is offset by a somewhat sluggish and underpowered moveset. A high rank Galarian Corsola has better neutral matchups than one with hatch IV's, so look to save your resources for the right one.

great.name: Shadow Altaria
great.notes: Moonblast and Sky Attack are now interchangeable, making Altaria more flexible than ever. Fairy + Fire coverage provides more super effective targets, including the mirror. Against Fire and Water types that resist both, Altaria can usually muscle through those matchups with its superior bulk. Altaria is still vulnerable to Ice, and its pacing a bit on the slower side.

great.name: Shadow Corviknight
great.notes: Corviknight receives damage buffs to both Air Cutter and Iron Head, improving its neutrals and giving it stronger identity. While its pacing is now slower, it's also less bait and boost dependent. It should be a strong contender going into the season. For those who find regular Corviknight lacking, Shadow Corviknight is worth serious consideration.

great.name: Florges
great.notes: Florges's mix of coverage gives it a unique matchup profile and technical play. Even Tinkaton hasn't stopped it from being a top used pick in competitive. Movesets can vary depending on your team and playstyle. Florges struggles against Dragons without a Fairy-type Charged Attack.

great.name: Shadow Quagsire
great.notes: Quagsire has the best bulk and pacing of its competition, making it a top meta pick. The Shadow is typically preferred. Its moveset has shifted between Mud Bomb and Stone Edge, with Mud Bomb making it stronger into Steel types and Stone Edge giving it coverage against Flying types.

great.name: Ninetales
great.notes: Kanto Ninetales has quickly risen as a top pick with a Worlds-winning pedigree. Its Energy Ball coverage is so effective that it has warped Water and Ground types around it. The Shadow is almost always preferred. Ninetales struggles against Dragons and rival Fire types, so build your team accordingly.

great.name: Quagsire
great.notes: Quagsire has the best bulk and pacing of its competition, making it a top meta pick. The Shadow is typically preferred. Its moveset has shifted between Mud Bomb and Stone Edge, with Mud Bomb making it stronger into Steel types and Stone Edge giving it coverage against Flying types.

great.name: Thievul
great.notes: Thievul has had a strong competitive debut, making the top usage charts at Worlds. This season buffs rival Dark types, which Thievul struggles against, so it may have more competition but it's still riding a wave from its Community Day.

great.name: Araquanid
great.notes: Araquanid gets a complete makeover in the Fast and Charged Attack departments. Infestation and Water Pulse are required to challenge Kanto Ninetales, while Mirror Coat is now its lowest energy move and actually viable. Araquanid's sheer bulk allows it to take on key meta targets. Its main threats are Flying types like Cramorant, so it pairs well with an Electric partner.

great.name: Clodsire
great.notes: Clodsire is never quite out of the meta and has always been a solid generalist. Its main drawbacks are its low Fast Attack pressure, pacing, and weaknesses to Ground, Ice, and Water.

great.name: Shadow Hydreigon
great.notes: Shadow Hydreigon has risen to prominence as high offense corebreaker. Its glassy stats and double weakness to Fairy make it a challenge to pilot, but it's proven itself on the competitive stage in expert hands.

great.name: Shadow Sableye
great.notes: Shadow Sableye has found renewed play with Drain Punch, of all things. This fast-paced Defense boost gives Sableye even more neutral play. This moveset is aggressive and technical, and requires significant practice to know which move to throw when.

great.name: Marowak
great.notes: Marowak maintains a strong presence in the metagame even after the Mud Slap nerf. The non-Shadow version has risen in popularity thanks to its ability to tank Grass-type coverage moves.

great.name: Stunfisk
great.notes: Stunfisk is a key meta player, strong against Steel types and Flying with great pacing and bulk. Its Charged Attacks aren't the strongest, so its neutral matchups leave something to be desired. Stunfisk forms tight team cores, giving it a more RPS playstyle.

great.name: Vigoroth
great.notes: Vigoroth has returned to terrorize veteran players, this time with STAB Scratch as its Fast Attack. It will be scrapping for Lickilicky's safe swap role, with less bulk than other Normal types but impressive damage output. Rock Slide has been its coverage move of choice in the past, but it can make use of Brick Brick or Bulldoze, too.

great.name: Jellicent
great.notes: Jellicent has everything you look for in a top Pokemon - excellent stats, typing, pacing, and power. Its diverse resistances make it a centerpiece for team building. Its biggest flaw is its vulnerability to Normal types. Jellicent takes a dip this season  as Shadow Ball is weaker and Dark types are stronger.

great.name: Empoleon
great.notes: Empoleon has enjoyed competitive success over the past several seasons, but has dire prospects into the newest Steel favorite, Melmetal. It sports strong pacing and Hydro Cannon's signature power, but with below average stat product. Empoleon has historically paired well with Altaria, able to cover its Fairy and Ice weaknesses.

great.name: Shadow Empoleon
great.notes: Empoleon has enjoyed competitive success over the past several seasons, but has dire prospects into the newest Steel favorite, Melmetal. It sports strong pacing and Hydro Cannon's signature power, but with below average stat product. Empoleon has historically paired well with Altaria, able to cover its Fairy and Ice weaknesses.

great.name: Fearow
great.notes: Fearow's solid pacing and great offenses make it a top Flying choice in the metagame. While it lacks bulk, its Normal typing is highly valuable against Great League's resident Ghost types.

great.name: Mantine
great.notes: Mantine saw significant play last season to combat Kanto Ninetales, but in the early runnings, it's largely been usurped by Cramorant. Mantine sports more bulk and coverage, but weaker offenses.

great.name: Snorlax
great.notes: Snorlax has reawakened with competitive pacing to fill Lickilicky's absence. It has has both Shadow and non-Shadow options to consider, plus multiple Charged Attack options. Superpower lays on the hurt against other Normal types while Earthquake is better into Tinkaton.

great.name: Umbreon
great.notes: Umbreon stands among the bulkiest Pokemon in the format. While its top meta days are behind it, Umbreon has improved potential with the Charm nerf and Dark Pulse buff. Its biggest draw is its ability to absorb damage and grind matches to a halt, serving as a pivot or tempo reset. Its offenses are completely lacking, so pair it with high pressure picks for the most synergy.

great.name: Shadow Araquanid
great.notes: Araquanid gets a complete makeover in the Fast and Charged Attack departments. Infestation and Water Pulse are required to challenge Kanto Ninetales, while Mirror Coat is now its lowest energy move and actually viable. Araquanid's sheer bulk allows it to take on key meta targets. Its main threats are Flying types like Cramorant, so it pairs well with an Electric partner.

great.name: Feraligatr
great.notes: Feraligatr is a longtime staple thanks to its powerful moveset. Shadow Claw shreds through ever-present Ghost types, and gives it a more neutral profile into other Waters. Preference for Shadow vs non-Shadow is split, currently leaning toward non-Shadow.

great.name: Annihilape
great.notes: Annihilape has maintained a small but constant presence as one of the lone viable Fighting types. This season, Low Kick should overtake Counter as the move of choice. Annihilape has multiple viable movesets, and must choose between coverage or closing power. Ice Punch has historically been preferred. Annihilape faces challenges this season from meta-defining Ghost and Flying types.

great.name: Azumarill
great.notes: Azumarill has withstood the test of time and remains one of Great League's most prominent mascots. It owes this to its extreme bulk and excellent defensive typing. Azumarill's main drawback is its pacing, which leaves it outsped by the format's more aggressive picks.

great.name: Deoxys (Defense)
great.notes: Defense Deoxys was a powerhouse in the early days of PvP, and is highly anticipated with multiple buffs this season. Sims don't capture its hit-and-run playstyle as a lead, which clears its Attack debuffs. While the buffs are impressive, it has an uphill battle against prominent Ghost and Dark types. Its biggest wins tend to be soft while its biggest losses are very, very hard.

great.name: Hisuian Electrode
great.notes: Hisuian Electrode made a statement at Worlds with strong usage and performance in even hard counter scenarios. Wild Charge packs enough punch to threaten Kanto Ninetales, while Energy Ball devastates Ground types that otherwise resist its Electric attacks. It may not have the bulk or defensive typing to remain a staple, but this little ball is in the right meta at the right time.

great.name: Rillaboom
great.notes: Rillaboom has been a smash hit this season thanks to energy generation from Scratch to pair with the insane power of Drum Beating. Rillaboom is glassy on its own, but Drum Beating's guaranteed debuff gives it much needed artificial bulk. Its pure Grass typing may limit its play against the core meta.

great.name: Sableye
great.notes: Sableye is a longtime staple which has more recently seen play in its Shadow form. Tinkaton is a severe threat, so its traditional role as a safe swap is no longer as safe. Still, its flexibility always offers a high degree of play. Return can't be regained once it's removed, so carefully consider your options before you TM it away.

great.name: Shadow Annihilape
great.notes: Annihilape has maintained a small but constant presence as one of the lone viable Fighting types. This season, Low Kick should overtake Counter as the move of choice. Annihilape has multiple viable movesets, and must choose between coverage or closing power. Ice Punch has historically been preferred. Annihilape faces challenges this season from meta-defining Ghost and Flying types.

great.name: Lapras
great.notes: Lapras has a long competitive history, but has been absent from the recent metagame. It's a poster child for bulky Water types and neutral play.

great.name: Shadow Snorlax
great.notes: Snorlax has reawakened with competitive pacing to fill Lickilicky's absence. It has has both Shadow and non-Shadow options to consider, and Superpower to lay on the hurt against other Normal types. Its matchups against Ghosts are more grueling, however.

great.name: Shadow Vigoroth
great.notes: Vigoroth has returned to terrorize veteran players, this time with STAB Scratch as its Fast Attack. It will be scrapping for Lickilicky's safe swap role, with less bulk than other Normal types but impressive damage output. Rock Slide has been its coverage move of choice in the past, but it can make use of Brick Brick or Bulldoze, too.

great.name: Charjabug
great.notes: Charjabug boasts decent stats and neutral play, which are hard to find among other Electric types. Its Bug typing softens its matchups against Ground types. This electric bus notably resists Melmetal's typical Charged Attacks, and can farm down Cramorant without ever triggering its Gulp Missile.

great.name: Malamar
great.notes: Our friend Malamar is a flexible Pokemon with decent competitive success. Quick pacing and reliable damage add to this Pokemon's unique typing. It performs best when Fighting and Poison types occupy the meta, which isn't often, and struggles into Fairies and other Dark types.

great.name: Furret
great.notes: Furret offers a safe pick with Fast Attack pressure and coverage into Water types. With Lickilicky out of the picture, it can fill in the Normal safe swap role, though it's been overtaken by Vigoroth in the early runnings.

great.name: Guzzlord
great.notes: Guzzlord is one of the most viable Dragon types behind Altaria. Its Dark typing gives it the edge against Ghosts and popular Normal types like Furret. With Wigglytuff nerfed, it has at least one less nightmare matchup to worry about. Guzzlord's insanely high stamina stat makes it resilient to low-damage Fast Attacks.

great.name: Shadow Malamar
great.notes: Our friend Malamar is a flexible Pokemon with decent competitive success. Quick pacing and reliable damage add to this Pokemon's unique typing. It performs best when Fighting and Poison types occupy the meta, which isn't often, and struggles into Fairies and other Dark types.

great.name: Carbink
great.notes: Carbink is the Fairy-type Bastiodon, but hasn't acquired quite the same notoriety or competitive success. Its slow pacing and prominent weaknesses make it difficult to use. It's seen increased usage to combat Kanto Ninetales and Thievul.

great.name: Shadow Charjabug
great.notes: Charjabug boasts decent stats and neutral play, which are hard to find among other Electric types. Its Bug typing softens its matchups against Ground types. This electric bus notably resists Melmetal's typical Charged Attacks, and can farm down Cramorant without ever triggering its Gulp Missile.

great.name: Dondozo
great.notes: Dondozo made a big splash at Worlds, outcompeting Milotic for a similar role. Its bulk makes up for its slower pacing and allows it to tank Grass coverage attacks. It's less flexible than other Water types, so it's better suited if you prefer playing for switch advantage.

great.name: Shadow Forretress
great.notes: Forretress has been a frontrunner in competitive play with great stats, typing, and coverage. The Shadow is typically preferred. Both Volt Switch and Bug Bite variants see competitive play. Forretress previously enjoyed Fire-free metagames, but Kanto Ninetales usage has surged so much that Forretress is in a riskier spot.

great.name: Hippowdon
great.notes: Hippowdon is now a World champion Pokemon. It's comparable to Kanto Marowak with a 1-turn Fast Attack and better pacing to its Rock-type coverage. The Shadow version has just enough bulk to survive Energy Ball from Shadow Kanto Ninetales, but the non-Shadow is a bit more comfortable in this matchup.

great.name: Mandibuzz
great.notes: Mandibuzz is the Flying Umbreon with sheer bulk on its side. It's failed to break into the open meta as of late, with Tinkaton as an ever-present threat. Where it falls short in the open league, it's always looking for carrion in themed cups where it can out-bulk smaller rosters.

great.name: Morpeko (Full Belly)
great.notes: Each time Morpeko uses any Charged Attack, Aura Wheel switches typing between Electric and Dark. Morpeko sees notable play in GBL where it can sweep teams that are unprepared for it. Its defenses crumble to even neutral Fast Attack pressure, so shields are required to spin this hamster wheel to victory. Despite infesting GBL, it's seen little to no tournament play.

great.name: Forretress
great.notes: Forretress has been a frontrunner in competitive play with great stats, typing, and coverage. The Shadow is typically preferred. Both Volt Switch and Bug Bite variants see competitive play. Forretress previously enjoyed Fire-free metagames, but Kanto Ninetales usage has surged so much that Forretress is in a riskier spot.

great.name: Medicham
great.notes: Medicham may not be at its previous heights, but has some viability among a thin Fighting roster. Its struggles against Ghost and Fairy remain, and its neutral matchups aren't as prolific as players remember.

great.name: Jumpluff
great.notes: Jumpluff can safely run its STAB moveset instead of its old dual-Flying set. With its extremely bulky stats, Jumpluff is a rare Grass type with relevance in the open meta. The non-Shadow is generally preferred since its moves are higher energy.

great.name: Kingdra
great.notes: Kingdra's typing gives it a strong neutral profile, but it lacks the bulk and resistances of more competitive picks like Altaria. Kingdra's niche is its dominating matchups against Fire types, which it double resists.

great.name: Blastoise
great.notes: Blastoise is the bulkiest Hydro Cannon user and can augment this even further with Skull Bash. With an excellent balance of stats, power, and speed, it occupies a small but strong spot in the metagame.

great.name: Diggersby
great.notes: Diggersby doesn't see much play despite its Normal typing and impressive stats. It's not best in class in either the Normal or Ground departments, and its Fire + Ground offenses are easily walled. Still, its sheer bulk means it shouldn't be underestimated.

great.name: Shadow Feraligatr
great.notes: Feraligatr is a longtime staple thanks to its powerful moveset. Shadow Claw shreds through ever-present Ghost types, and gives it a more neutral profile into other Waters. Preference for Shadow vs non-Shadow is split, currently leaning toward non-Shadow.

great.name: Shadow Hippowdon
great.notes: Hippowdon is now a World champion Pokemon. It's comparable to Kanto Marowak with a 1-turn Fast Attack and better pacing to its Rock-type coverage. The Shadow version has just enough bulk to survive Energy Ball from Shadow Kanto Ninetales, but the non-Shadow is a bit more comfortable in this matchup.

great.name: Shadow Kingdra
great.notes: Kingdra's typing gives it a strong neutral profile, but it lacks the bulk and resistances of more competitive picks like Altaria. Kingdra's niche is its dominating matchups against Fire types, which it double resists.

great.name: Shadow Lapras
great.notes: Lapras has a long competitive history, but has been absent from the recent metagame. It's a poster child for bulky Water types and neutral play.

great.name: Turtonator
great.notes: Turtonator usually excels in themed cups, but has a niche as a hard counter to Kanto Ninetales. Overheat gives it closing power in neutral matchups while Dragon Claw is an option for more rounded coverage.

great.name: Pachirisu
great.notes: The elusive Pachirisu has some of the most bulk among Electric types. The only thing it lacks is meaningful coverage, which can be played around with the right team. There are generally more flexible (and accessible) picks.

great.name: Cradily
great.notes: Cradily thrives by piling Attack drops onto its natural bulk. It works best in the backline where it can make those Attack drops stick. It has three viable Fast Attacks—Acid is the most well rounded, while Bullet Seed and Infestation can target specific matchups.

great.name: Shadow Dragonair
great.notes: Dragonair is a fast-paced, aggressive pick. Despite its offensive strengths, it falls short of rival Dragons like Altaria, Guzzlord, and Kingdra in terms of bulk and resistances. Because of this, it hasn't seen widespread play in a while, but watch for it in Dragon-centered metas. The Shadow is almost always preferred.

great.name: Alolan Ninetales
great.notes: The sims don't always use Chilling Water optimally, so Alolan Ninetales should perform better in some head to head matchups than indicated.

great.name: Dewgong
great.notes: Dewgong has a long competitive history thanks to its bulk and Icy Wind debuffs. It typically underperforms in the sims, where its full game effects aren't well represented. A reworked Drill Run further improves its pacing and damage output, making Dewgong a prospect to watch for.

great.name: Shadow Dusclops
great.notes: Dusclops doesn't see much play over more competitive Ghosts like Galarian Corsola or Jellicent. It's still viable in its own right, with great stats and pacing.

great.name: Galarian Moltres
great.notes: Galarian Moltres has seen better days, with a mix of meta developments pushing it out of the top Flying spot. Its stats are more tempered than Mandibuzz, so it has to watch for coverage and commit to shields.

great.name: Shadow Alolan Ninetales
great.notes: The sims don't always use Chilling Water optimally, so Alolan Ninetales should perform better in some head to head matchups than indicated.

great.name: Hydreigon
great.notes: Shadow Hydreigon has risen to prominence as high offense corebreaker. Its glassy stats and double weakness to Fairy make it a challenge to pilot, but it's proven itself on the competitive stage in expert hands. The normal version doesn't see the same play.

great.name: Doublade
great.notes: Doublade has its share of doubters. Despite Shadow Claw, Sacred Sword, and amazing typing, Doublade has yet to prove its sum is greater than the parts. Compared to Aegislash, it's more reliable and less technical, but its higher floor also comes with a lower ceiling in terms of impact.

great.name: Dusclops
great.notes: Dusclops doesn't see much play over more competitive Ghosts like Galarian Corsola or Jellicent. It's still viable in its own right, with great stats and pacing.

great.name: Swampert
great.notes: Swampert carries a winning legacy since the earliest days of PvP. It has some renewed play, but is firmly behind Quagsire in usage.

great.name: Shadow Swampert
great.notes: Swampert carries a winning legacy since the earliest days of PvP. It has some renewed play, but is firmly behind Quagsire in usage.

great.name: Aegislash (Blade)
great.notes: It's taken a while, but players are finally finding success with Aegislash in competitive. Its unique mechanics can feel clunky and take dedication to master. Mimikyu's debut hampers Aegislash viability, as Aegislash is completely thwarted by it. Before powering up, make sure to check your Aegislash's IV ranks in both forms.

great.name: Shadow Marowak
great.notes: Marowak maintains a strong presence in the metagame even after the Mud Slap nerf. The non-Shadow version has risen in popularity thanks to its ability to tank Grass-type coverage moves.

great.name: Seismitoad
great.notes: Seismitoad provides a shakeup as a new Water/Ground contender. It's neither the bulkiest or hardest hitting in that category, but it makes up for it in the sheer utility of Icy Wind. With a steady 5 pacing, Icy Wind is a direct threat to its only weakness (Grass), and throws a wrench into popular team cores.

great.name: Talonflame
great.notes: It's been a hot minute since Talonflame has seen widepsread play. Since Water is a constant threat, Kanto Ninetales has become the ubiquitous Fire type. The new mechanics which prioritize Charged Attacks over Fast Attacks also hurt long duration attacks like Incinerate. Talonflame is still plenty viable, just not a top choice.

great.name: Dragonair
great.notes: Dragonair is a fast-paced, aggressive pick. Despite its offensive strengths, it falls short of rival Dragons like Altaria, Guzzlord, and Kingdra in terms of bulk and resistances. Because of this, it hasn't seen widespread play in a while, but watch for it in Dragon-centered metas. The Shadow is almost always preferred.

great.name: Gourgeist (Large)
great.notes: Gourgeist is an alternate Grass option with its truly unique moveset. As a Ghost, it also operates as a solid generalist. However, key Normal types fill the generalist role better and threaten Gourgeist in return. Gourgeist works best as a surprise corebreaker with ample  support against Normal and Flying.

great.name: Registeel
great.notes: Registeel is a relic from the ancient past. Its stats are still legendary, but it now faces a much stronger field. Registeel's complete lack of Fast Attack pressure means it must rely on Charged Attacks to KO, making it challenging to play. While it has some promising matchups, skepticism is warranted as modern meta picks can dance in circles around it.

great.name: Shadow Steelix
great.notes: Thunder Fang plus debuffing attacks give Steelix a unique role. The Shadow boost helps make up for its lack of STAB, but it still struggles with its minimal shield pressure and closing power. Look to pair it with strong offensive pressure and Pokemon that can capitalize on alignment.

great.name: Gourgeist (Super)
great.notes: Gourgeist is an alternate Grass option with its truly unique moveset. As a Ghost, it also operates as a solid generalist. However, key Normal types fill the generalist role better and threaten Gourgeist in return. Gourgeist works best as a surprise corebreaker with ample  support against Normal and Flying.

great.name: Grumpig
great.notes: Grumpig's stats and typing are nothing to write home about, its Ghost + Fighting offenses are enough to make it a flexible choice. The Shadow Ball nerf will reduce its already meager usage.

great.name: Clefable
great.notes: Meteor Mash gives Clefable strong play into other Fairies. However, it faces stiff competition and usually takes a backseat to more well rounded options.

great.name: Gourgeist (Average)
great.notes: Gourgeist is an alternate Grass option with its truly unique moveset. As a Ghost, it also operates as a solid generalist. However, key Normal types fill the generalist role better and threaten Gourgeist in return. Gourgeist works best as a surprise corebreaker with ample  support against Normal and Flying.

great.name: Oranguru
great.notes: Oranguru has solid stats and a neutral type profile. Confusion gives it a clunky playstyle. It's frequently a top pick in themed cups, but doesn't see play in open competition, where Psychic damage is less valuable and it's eclipsed by other Normal types.

great.name: Shadow Drapion
great.notes: Drapion sports neutral typing and a signature fast pace. Prominent Steel types keep it from achieving its past potential. Shadow Drapion is typically preferred over the normal version.

great.name: Gourgeist (Small)
great.notes: Gourgeist is an alternate Grass option with its truly unique moveset. As a Ghost, it also operates as a solid generalist. However, key Normal types fill the generalist role better and threaten Gourgeist in return. Gourgeist works best as a surprise corebreaker with ample  support against Normal and Flying.

great.name: Shadow Talonflame
great.notes: It's been a hot minute since Talonflame has seen widepsread play. Since Water is a constant threat, Kanto Ninetales has become the ubiquitous Fire type. The new mechanics which prioritize Charged Attacks over Fast Attacks also hurt long duration attacks like Incinerate. Talonflame is still plenty viable, just not a top choice.

great.name: Samurott
great.notes: Samurott looks great on paper, and while it's by no means a bad pick, it lacks the competitive success and neutral play of its peers. Its Bug offenses are its main detriment and are widely resisted by the main meta players.

great.name: Wigglytuff
great.notes: While Wigglytuff's neutral matchups are dialed back, the hard counter role it's known for still remains. It's better suited for themed cups now than open competition.

great.name: Walrein
great.notes: Walrein has a notable competitive past, but hasn't found a way to crack the current metagame. Its time may come again, but faces too much competition against rival Water types, including its pre-evolution, Sealeo.

great.name: Steelix
great.notes: Shadow Steelix is typically preferred over the regular variant for additional Fast Attack pressure and the boost to its non-STAB attacks.

great.name: Spiritomb
great.notes: Spiritomb sees far less play than its counterpart, Sableye. Its pacing is considerably slow in a meta that is growing ever faster. In particular, this means it can't take full advantage of Rock Tomb's debuffs.

great.name: Shadow Walrein
great.notes: Walrein has a notable competitive past, but hasn't found a way to crack the current metagame. Its time may come again, but faces too much competition against rival Water types, including its pre-evolution, Sealeo.

great.name: Zweilous
great.notes: Guzzlord is preferred over Zweilous with its slightly better stats and Poison coverage into Fairy counters.

great.name: Shadow Metang
great.notes: Metang has good stats and pacing, but has struggled to find competitive success. It struggles significantly against rival Steel types, and its Psychic typing makes it vulnerable to prevalent Ghosts.

great.name: Metang
great.notes: Metang has good stats and pacing, but has struggled to find competitive success. It struggles significantly against rival Steel types, and its Psychic typing makes it vulnerable to prevalent Ghosts.

great.name: Shadow Zweilous
great.notes: Guzzlord is preferred over Zweilous with its slightly better stats and Poison coverage into Fairy counters.

great.name: Bastiodon
great.notes: Bastiodon is seemingly extinct after a long reign of terror. It's the sheer definition of bulk with a win hard, lose hard playstyle. The metagame has turbocharged ahead of it, so it'll need a major revival to see contention.

ultra.name: Corviknight
ultra.notes: Ultra League gives Corviknight more room to flex its bulk. It pairs excellently with other top picks, making it a team building centerpiece. Stronger damage for Air Cutter and Iron Head improve its previously weak output.

ultra.name: Shadow Corviknight
ultra.notes: Ultra League gives Corviknight more room to flex its bulk. It pairs excellently with other top picks, making it a team building centerpiece. Stronger damage for Air Cutter and Iron Head improve its previously weak output.

ultra.name: Virizion
ultra.notes: Virizion has a long pedigree in Ultra League. Its hard wins against Water and Steel types outweigh its lack of flexibility, although Stone Edge is always an option. With Talonflame and Giratina on a significant downturn, it is perhaps at its most meta relevant ever.

ultra.name: Empoleon
ultra.notes: Impressive typing and pacing make Empoleon a standout Hydro Cannon user in the format. It's found stronger meta relevancy here in Ultra League, where a wider abundance of Dragon and Fairy types see play. Its lower stat product can easily be shored up by the format's higher bulk and prominent stat-reducing attacks.

ultra.name: Shadow Empoleon
ultra.notes: Impressive typing and pacing make Empoleon a standout Hydro Cannon user in the format. It's found stronger meta relevancy here in Ultra League, where a wider abundance of Dragon and Fairy types see play. Its lower stat product can easily be shored up by the format's higher bulk and prominent stat-reducing attacks.

ultra.name: Mimikyu
ultra.notes:
Mimikyu's special ability blocks the first unshielded Charged Attack it receives; its Defense then lowers by 1 stage the rest of the match, even if it swaps out.

This effectively grants Mimikyu a third shield, a massive advantage that far outweighs its drawbacks. It performs best when given shields to delay the debuff.

Even with Shadow Sneak and middling stats, Mimikyu's head-to-head matchups are head and shoulders above anything else in PvP. Its neutral typing and Ghost/Fairy coverage further help it excel as a generalist. The only thing reducing its score is that it's an unknown commodity - we'll see if it has the team success it does in the sims.

ultra.name: Florges
ultra.notes: Florges is a top meta contender even in the face of Tinkaton. Stat effects from either Chilling Water or Trailblaze give it more technical play.

ultra.name: Galarian Moltres
ultra.notes: Galarian Moltres is still a strong contender in Ultra League, but the Tinkaton's ubiquity poses a major challenge for it.

ultra.name: Shadow Feraligatr
ultra.notes: Feraligatr is a longtime staple thanks to its powerful moveset. Shadow Claw shreds through ever-present Ghost types, and gives it a more neutral profile into other Waters.

ultra.name: Feraligatr
ultra.notes: Feraligatr is a longtime staple thanks to its powerful moveset. Shadow Claw shreds through ever-present Ghost types, and gives it a more neutral profile into other Waters.

ultra.name: Jellicent
ultra.notes: One of the top Water types, Jellicent stands out with excellent bulk and pacing. Its closing power is now slightly reduced with the Shadow Ball nerf.

ultra.name: Giratina (Altered)
ultra.notes: Once the mascot of the format, Giratina's play has declined in recent seasons. It is weak to both of its sub-typings and no longer stands out as the best Ghost or the best Dragon. Even so, it's still plenty competitive. The regular version has the longest tenure and can make more reliable use of Shadow Force.

ultra.name: Cramorant
ultra.notes: Cramorant falls just short of the Ultra League CP limit, but its special mechanics help it punch above its weight. The percentage damage from Gulp Missile can soften bulky targets and opponents that otherwise resist its moves.

ultra.name: Guzzlord
ultra.notes: Guzzlord sees notable play in Ultra League where it provides valuable resistance to Water. Proper team building and a focus on alignment are required to escape its debilitating Fairy weakness.

ultra.name: Skeledirge
ultra.notes: Skeledirge is the premiere Fire type of Ultra League, with excellent power, coverage, and accessibility. Disarming Voice is an option to hit back against Dark and Dragon-type counters.

ultra.name: Lapras
ultra.notes: Lapras is a solid choice for Ultra League, although it takes a back seat to other Water types like Jellicent and Feraligatr, which perform better into one another.

ultra.name: Shadow Lapras
ultra.notes: Lapras is a solid choice for Ultra League, although it takes a back seat to other Water types like Jellicent and Feraligatr, which perform better into one another.

ultra.name: Alolan Ninetales
ultra.notes: The sims don't always use Chilling Water optimally, so Alolan Ninetales should perform better in some head to head matchups than indicated. Chilling Water is a sidegrade, if not a slight improvement which gives Alolan Ninetales coverage against Fire and broader technical play.

ultra.name: Dusknoir
ultra.notes: Dusknoir combines offensive pressure and great coverage in a strong Ghost-type package. It may not see as much play as more established Ghosts, like Giratina or Drifblim. The Shadow version is typically preferred for the additional pressure.

ultra.name: Dondozo
ultra.notes: Dondozo adds to the roster of bulky Water types. It hasn't seen widespread play yet, falling behind faster and more flexible picks.

ultra.name: Shadow Dusknoir
ultra.notes: Dusknoir combines offensive pressure and great coverage in a strong Ghost-type package. It may not see as much play as more established Ghosts, like Giratina or Drifblim. The Shadow version is typically preferred for the additional pressure.

ultra.name: Registeel
ultra.notes: Registeel has a storied history in Ultra League. As power creep has made other Pokemon faster and stronger, Registeel is mostly a relic from a bygone age. Its playstyle is difficult to master - it has no Fast Attack pressure and relies solely on its high energy Charged Attacks to secure knockouts. While it could still succeed, its place in the metagame has fallen by the wayside.

ultra.name: Shadow Alolan Ninetales
ultra.notes: The sims don't always use Chilling Water optimally, so Alolan Ninetales should perform better in some head to head matchups than indicated. Chilling Water is a sidegrade, if not a slight improvement which gives Alolan Ninetales coverage against Fire and broader technical play.

ultra.name: Forretress
ultra.notes: Similar to Great League, Ultra League Forretress has a sluggish moveset, but even more bulk to work with its debuffing attacks.

ultra.name: Shadow Giratina (Altered)
ultra.notes: Once the mascot of the format, Giratina's play has declined in recent seasons. It is weak to both of its sub-typings and no longer stands out as the best Ghost or the best Dragon. Even so, it's still plenty competitive. The regular version has the longest tenure and can make more reliable use of Shadow Force.

ultra.name: Regidrago
ultra.notes: Regidrago is a powerful Dragon options with its hard hitting exclusive move. Its poor coverage and average stats keep it from truly excelling.

ultra.name: Cresselia
ultra.notes: As one of the longest running mascots of Ultra League, Cresselia could see some resurgence but has thus far failed to find a foothold in the metagame. Top picks like  Corviknight pose major resistance, while its Psychic typing generally hurts it in a format that favors Dark and Ghost types. Still, its stats alone keep it competitive if overshadowed by power creep over the years.

ultra.name: Talonflame
ultra.notes: Talonflame is a longtime staple of Ultra League. The prominence of Water and Dragon types keeps it from dominating, but it serves a vital role against the format's Steel types.

ultra.name: Shadow Forretress
ultra.notes: Similar to Great League, Ultra League Forretress has a sluggish moveset, but even more bulk to work with its debuffing attacks.

ultra.name: Runerigus
ultra.notes: Access to Rock Tomb allows Runerigus to shine in Ultra League, where it takes more advantage of its bulk. As such, it's quickly established itself in the metagame. Without Ground-type offenses, it functions more as a neutral pick than a true Ground type like Gastrodon. Its Water weakness can be a liability.

ultra.name: Shadow Walrein
ultra.notes: Walrein is a viable and accessible pick, but hasn't resumed its past domination. Jellicent and Feraligatr are more strongly favored in the Water category.

ultra.name: Deoxys (Defense)
ultra.notes: Defense Deoxys was a powerhouse in the early days of PvP, and is highly anticipated with multiple buffs this season. Sims don't capture its hit-and-run playstyle which clears its Attack debuffs. While it's hard to ignore the sheer numbers, Psychic typing is a disadvantage and Deoxys may struggle against the power creep since its heyday.

ultra.name: Steelix
ultra.notes: Steelix's unusual mix of fantastic stats, solid typing, and non-STAB attacks give it an unusual role in the metagame. It can power through matchups in unintuitive ways, but its lack of shield pressure and closing power can be more apparent in Ultra League where it faces bulkier targets.

ultra.name: Walrein
ultra.notes: Walrein is a viable and accessible pick, but hasn't resumed its past domination. Jellicent and Feraligatr are more strongly favored in the Water category.

ultra.name: Shadow Cresselia
ultra.notes: As one of the longest running mascots of Ultra League, Cresselia could see some resurgence but has thus far failed to find a foothold in the metagame. Top picks like  Corviknight pose major resistance, while its Psychic typing generally hurts it in a format that favors Dark and Ghost types. Still, its stats alone keep it competitive if overshadowed by power creep over the years.

ultra.name: Shadow Steelix
ultra.notes: Steelix's unusual mix of fantastic stats, solid typing, and non-STAB attacks give it an unusual role in the metagame. It can power through matchups in unintuitive ways, but its lack of shield pressure and closing power can be more apparent in Ultra League where it faces bulkier targets.

ultra.name: Ampharos
ultra.notes: Ampharos has overtaken Bellibolt as the Electric type of choice, and has a long history in Ultra League. It combines speed and valuable coverage, although its stat product is a bit lacking.

ultra.name: Shadow Cradily
ultra.notes: Cradily is not as omnipresent in Ultra League, but still a formidable pick. The format's bulk improves its play with Rock Tomb. However, it faces some sterner resistance, particularly from Empoleon, Virizion, and Zygarde.

ultra.name: Shadow Ampharos
ultra.notes: Ampharos has overtaken Bellibolt as the Electric type of choice, and has a long history in Ultra League. It combines speed and valuable coverage, although its stat product is a bit lacking.

ultra.name: Shadow Talonflame
ultra.notes: Talonflame is a longtime staple of Ultra League. The prominence of Water and Dragon types keeps it from dominating, but it serves a vital role against the format's Steel types.

ultra.name: Bellibolt
ultra.notes: Bellibolt has reduced pacing with Parabolic Charge, but is still a viable pick. Its usage has largely been overtaken by Ampharos.

ultra.name: Doublade
ultra.notes: Doublade has yet to see competitive success in any league, so there are many reasons to be skeptical of its Ultra League prospects. The resources required to build it are better invested in its evolution, Aegislash.

ultra.name: Grumpig
ultra.notes: Grumpig sports solid stats and coveted FIghting + Ghost coverage. However, it shares similar struggles to Cresselia and has thus fair failed to find a place in the metagame. Its Psychic typing puts it at a general disadvantage in a meta that favors Ghost and Dark types. All in all, Grumpig has some noteworthy traits but a lot left to prove.

ultra.name: Shadow Grumpig
ultra.notes: Grumpig sports solid stats and coveted FIghting + Ghost coverage. However, it shares similar struggles to Cresselia and has thus fair failed to find a place in the metagame. Its Psychic typing puts it at a general disadvantage in a meta that favors Ghost and Dark types. All in all, Grumpig has some noteworthy traits but a lot left to prove.

master.name: Palkia (Origin)
master.notes: Origin Palkia is one of the definitive Master League Pokemon. It has everything you could ask for - stats, speed, power, and great typing, making it a top pick by most categories. Origin Forme is strictly better than Palkia's regular forme. If you don't have Spacial Rend, Fire Blast is a viable option to hit Zacian and other Steel types.

master.name: Zacian (Crowned Sword)
master.notes: Crowned Forme Zacian boasts one of the best defensive typings in the game and stats which rival those of Mega Evolutions. It's a definitive Master League Pokemon of the current era, alongside Palkia. It's only held back by slower pacing and widely resisted Steel offenses, but neither of these put a dent in its dominating presence.

master.name: Kyurem (White)
master.notes: Black and White Kyurem have declined since the introduction of Zacian, but remain powerful picks. They capitalize on their amazing stats, solid pacing, and powerful signature attacks. White Kyurem is generally the less flexible of the two, but poses a stronger threat to Zacian and Palkia.

master.name: Kyogre
master.notes: Kyogre has always been a meta staple, but is in it's strongest shape ever thanks to a boost to Waterfall's energy generation and Avalanche coverage against Dragons. Origin Pulse is its best attack for neutral matchups, while Thunder is a coverage option that's more likely to see use in Mega Master League.

master.name: Dialga (Origin)
master.notes: Origin Dialga is a signature presence in Master League, strictly better than its regular forme. Iron Head is a weaker attack, so Dialga is more dependent on its nuke, Roar of Time, than Palkia is. Dialga's struggles against Zacian keep it from being as dominating as its predecessor.

master.name: Kyurem (Black)
master.notes: Black and White Kyurem have declined since the introduction of Zacian, but remain powerful picks. They capitalize on their amazing stats, solid pacing, and powerful signature attacks. Black Kyurem is generally the more flexible of the two but has fewer domineering matchups.

master.name: Lugia
master.notes: Lugia scores well in simulations thanks to its incredible stats and neutral matchup profile. It finally has coverage to hit Steel types at the cost of a little speed, an exchange Lugia is more than happy to make. Its Psychic typing puts it in the crossfire of Lunala and Lunala's counters, so prepare accordingly.

master.name: Lunala
master.notes: Lunala has risen as a Master League powerhouse despite its double weaknesses. Ghost + Fairy coverage is as perfect as you can get, so this Pokemon packs a ton of neutral shield pressure. The only thing it doesn't have over Dawn Wings Necrozma (yet) is that super powerful Moongeist Beam.

master.name: Shadow Lugia
master.notes: Lugia scores well in simulations thanks to its incredible stats and neutral matchup profile. It finally has coverage to hit Steel types at the cost of a little speed, an exchange Lugia is more than happy to make. Its Psychic typing puts it in the crossfire of Lunala and Lunala's counters, so prepare accordingly.

master.name: Ho-Oh
master.notes: Ho-oh is a vital anti-meta presence to combat Zacian and other Steel or Fairy types. Its high-energy attacks can threaten most Pokemon, but some may find its playstyle to be too cumbersome. It also faces significant challenges against Palkia.

master.name: Solgaleo
master.notes: Solgaleo's Steel typing and unique offenses give it an intriguing place in the metagame. However, its lack of closing power is a serious hindrance, and it's more likely to consume more shields than it earns. It can work as an anti-meta pick and on alignment heavy teams, but it lends a difficult win-more playstyle.

master.name: Primarina
master.notes: Primarina's stats may be eclipsed by its Legendary opponents, but it serves a vital and accessible anti-meta role against Palkia. Primarina depends on shields for success, so look to pair it with stat monsters who can absorb hits on its behalf.
